title: 5 farmer carries Mistakes That Are Destroying Your grip endurance
description: Pick up something heavy in each hand and walk. Your carry distance exposes grip endurance that no hang can measure. These five mistakes end most carries early. Here is the hundred-metre test, why your grip fades on the move, and the fixes that double your distance.

scenes.narration: Here is your test. Find two heavy objects, one for each hand. Water jugs, loaded backpacks, buckets of books, anything with a handle you can close your fingers around. Pick them up, stand tall, and start walking. Walk until your grip opens or your fingers simply refuse, and measure the DISTANCE. That is your carry number. No bar, no gym, no excuses. Keep the number. At the end of this video I will show you the five mistakes that end most carries in the first fifty metres, and exactly what your distance says about the cables in your forearms.

scenes.label: THE HUNDRED-METRE LINE
scenes.sub: under 40 m: untrained - 100 m: wired - 200 m: elite
scenes.narration: Here is the line. One hundred METRES of loaded walking before the grip gives up. Under forty metres, your grip endurance is simply untrained, and carries will fix it faster than almost anything. Forty to one hundred, you are building, but the fade still owns the second half of every walk. One hundred to two hundred, your cables hold like a farmhand's, steady under load for minutes at a time. Past two hundred metres, that is elite carrying grip. Distance is the honest score here, because you cannot fake a single metre of it.

Why does carrying feel different from hanging? On the bar, the load is still. In a carry, every step SLAMS the load up and down. Each footstep sends a small shock through the handle, and your fingers must re-grip, microsecond by microsecond, hundreds of times. The force is still made in the forearm and shipped through the tendons, but now the cables work like shock absorbers that can never switch off. That constant re-gripping is why carries build a kind of endurance hangs cannot: grip that survives movement, sweat and time all at once. Grip coaches divide grip into families, and the carry belongs to the SUPPORT family: the fingers wrapped and holding, the thumb locked over, the hand acting as a hook that must not open. Support grip is the most trainable and the most transferable of the families, because nearly every pulling movement you will ever do ends in exactly this position. When your support grip fades on a carry, it is also fading on your last deadlift, your last row, your last climb. The distance test is secretly a report on all of them.

beats.title: THE MOVING LOAD
lines: Each footstep forces a micro re-grip.

scenes.narration: The science of the carry fade is the same villain as the hang: blood flow. A gripping forearm squeezes its own vessels shut, and walking adds a second problem, because the load swings and the grip must spike again and again to catch it. Every spike costs blood flow you do not have. This is why smart carriers use the minimum grip that keeps the handle seated, and why your distance collapses when you white-knuckle from the first step. Trained carriers are not stronger squeezers. They are calmer ones, holding tension low and steady while the legs do the travelling. One asymmetry shows up in almost every first test: one hand quits early. The dominant side usually wins, but not always, because grip endurance follows use, not handedness. Note which hand opened first today. On training days, let the weak hand set the distance: when it fades, the set ends, and it gets the same work as the strong side instead of a smaller share. Within a month the gap narrows, and your total distance jumps, because a carry is only ever as long as its weaker hand.

There is a second system carries expose that hangs never touch: your POSTURE under grip load. When the forearms fade, the shoulders roll forward, the traps shrug up to the ears, and the whole chain starts leaking force. Strong carriers look boring. Chest tall, shoulders down, arms hanging like hooks from a frame that does not move. The grip is only the last link. If the frame above it collapses, the best tendons in the world still drop the load. Train the carry and you train the whole chain at once, which is why old-school strongmen called it the single most honest exercise they knew.

beats.text: THE GRIP IS THE LAST LINK

beats.title: THE BORING FRAME
lines: Shoulders down, chest tall, arms like hooks.

scenes.narration: The handle you choose is a hidden difficulty setting. A thin handle lets the fingers close almost fully, the strongest position the hand owns. A thick handle forces the fingers open, and open-hand gripping is dramatically weaker, which is why fat-grip tools humble everyone. Smooth handles slide and demand constant re-gripping; textured ones bite and help. For your test, use the same two objects every time, and write down what they weigh. A carry test with mystery weight is a story, not a measurement. When the same load starts feeling light, the honest progressions are simple: heavier objects, thicker handles, or a longer route.

beats.title: OPEN HAND = WEAK HAND
lines: Thick handles force the fingers open.

scenes.narration: And here is your advantage, because it is a big one. Carries punish total load, and total load includes YOU. A heavy man carrying heavy jugs is asking his grip to manage his own mass plus the iron, every step, while his bigger forearms burn oxygen faster. You carry the same jugs with a lighter frame and a smaller engine to feed. Pound for pound, skinny guys routinely out-carry men with arms twice their size, and it confuses everyone watching. Let it. Your grip endurance was never about the size of the arm. It is about how long the cables hold, and yours get to practise at a discount.
Carry with me. Pick them up, walk forty seconds, rest twenty, four rounds. Tall chest, shoulders down, calm grip. Let the legs do the work. Go.

Now the five mistakes. Mistake one: going too LIGHT. Carries only build grip endurance when the load threatens your grip in under two minutes. If you can stroll forever, it is cardio, not cable work. Mistake two: the death grip from step one. Crush the handles at the start and you spend your whole blood-flow budget before the halfway mark. Mistake three: shrugging to your ears. The moment the traps take over, the frame leaks and the grip pays for it. Mistake four: racing. Fast steps multiply the shocks. Walk like you are carrying full buckets you refuse to spill. Mistake five: setting the load down at the first burn. The burn is where the adaptation lives. Slow down, breathe, and buy ten more metres before you stop.

So, your distance. Under forty metres: untrained grip endurance, and the good news is carries respond faster than almost any quality we test here. Forty to one hundred: you are BUILDING, and the five fixes are written for you. One hundred to two hundred: WIRED, a working grip that holds under movement and time. Past two hundred: elite carrier territory. Drop your distance in the comments, just the metres. In thirty days we walk this test again with the same load, and the extra distance will be the receipt for every carry you did.

Thirty days, same load, same route, and the distance will tell the truth about your training. Subscribe, because every week we test another cable the mirror cannot see. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
